<section id="antarctica" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">01 / ANTARCTIC SUBGLACIAL GEOPHYSICS</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>A water-rich sedimentary aquifer beneath the South Pole</h2>
<p class="question">How much water is stored beneath the Antarctic interior-and where is the water stored?</p>
<p>Subglacial water is often considered in the form of lakes, channels, and thin films at the ice–bed interface. But porous sediments may host a much larger and longer-lived groundwater reservoir. 
To investigate this hidden component of the Antarctic hydrologic system, we deployed more than 500 seismic nodes along four transects extending up to 250 km from the South Pole.</p>
<p>Teleseismic receiver functions reveal a coherent negative-polarity conversion beneath the ice across large portions of the array. The observed waveforms cannot be explained by a simple ice-over-crystalline-bedrock structure and instead require a laterally extensive low-velocity layer. Waveform inversion shows that this layer is highly heterogeneous, ranging from tens of meters to several kilometers thick, with near-bed shear-wave velocities substantially lower than expected for compact crystalline basement.</p>
</div>

<section id="continental" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">02 / CONTINENTAL SEISMIC IMAGING &amp; JOINT INVERSION</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>More information.<br>Better constraints.</h2>
<p class="question">How can multiple seismic observables reduce ambiguity in crustal imaging?</p>
<p>Surface waves provide strong constraints on absolute shear-wave velocity, while receiver functions are sensitive to velocity contrasts and discontinuities such as the Moho. Yet even their joint inversion can leave important trade-offs among deep-crustal shear velocity, Moho depth, and crustal Vp/Vs.</p>
<p>In my 2024 JGR: Solid Earth study, I developed a Bayesian Monte Carlo approach that incorporates H–κ stacking into the joint inversion of surface-wave dispersion and receiver functions. By adding the arrival-time information carried by receiver-function multiples, the method substantially reduces these parameter trade-offs and allows crustal Vp/Vs to be constrained directly rather than assumed.</p>
<p>Applied across the northwestern United States, the resulting models reveal geologically coherent variations in crustal and uppermost-mantle structure. Elevated crustal Vp/Vs along coastal Oregon may reflect mafic composition or the presence of fluids, while variations in uppermost-mantle Vs closely follow independent estimates of Moho temperature. These results illustrate how improved constraints on seismic structure can provide information about crustal composition and thermal conditions.</p>

<section id="computational" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">03 / COMPUTATIONAL GEOPHYSICS &amp; UNCERTAINTY</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>Beyond a single best-fitting model.</h2>
<p class="question">Which features are well constrained—and where does uncertainty remain?</p>
<p>Geophysical imaging requires both efficient computation and a clear understanding of model uncertainty. My computational work spans Monte Carlo and Bayesian inversion, large-scale seismic data processing, and HPC/GPU workflows.</p>
<p>During a research internship at TGS in summer 2026, I developed and productionized Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) workflows for uncertainty quantification in 3-D/4-D acoustic full-waveform inversion.</p>
</div>

<section id="ongoing" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">04 / ONGOING RESEARCH</p>
<h2>Ongoing research</h2>

<article>
<h3>Layered crustal V<sub>P</sub>/V<sub>S</sub> and possible partial melting beneath the western United States</h3>
<p>I am extending seismic joint inversion to incorporate Rayleigh-wave local amplification and H/V ratios, with the goal of resolving depth-dependent crustal V<sub>P</sub>/V<sub>S</sub>. Using imaging results from the western United States, I am investigating whether the inferred lower-crustal properties are consistent with partial melting, while considering alternative interpretations and uncertainties.</p>
</article>

<article>
<h3>Diffusion models for receiver-function quality control</h3>
<p>I am exploring diffusion models for quality control of receiver functions, with the aim of developing a more consistent and scalable approach to assessing waveform quality for seismic imaging.</p>
</article>

<article>
<h3>A seismic reference model for the US continental crust</h3>
<p>I am also working on a seismic reference model for the U.S. continental crust with the newly developed method and new data.</p>
</article>
